questions.q: Which of these numbers is prime?
questions.e: 1 is not prime by definition, 9 = 3 × 3 and 21 = 3 × 7. 23 has no divisors other than 1 and itself.

questions.q: To check whether n is prime, the loop only needs to try divisors up to:
questions.e: Every composite n has a divisor of at most √n, so if none is found up to √n, n is prime.
The pairs (1,36), (2,18), (3,12), (4,9) add 2 each, and 6 × 6 adds 1 because it is the same number: 4 × 2 + 1 = 9.

questions.q: In the sieve, why does the inner loop start at i × i?
o: Smaller multiples were already crossed out by smaller primes
Starting at 2 × i gives a wrong answer
questions.e: Each multiple k × i with k < i has a smaller prime factor that already crossed it out. Starting at 2 × i still works; it just repeats work.

questions.q: What is the time complexity of the Sieve of Eratosthenes up to n?
questions.e: The prime p crosses out about n / p numbers, and the sum of n / p over the primes grows like n log log n: almost linear.

questions.q: Why write i * i <= n instead of i <= sqrt(n)?
o: sqrt() works with decimals and can be off by one
questions.e: sqrt() returns a double and can give 5.99999 instead of 6. With large n, use long long for i so that i * i doesn't overflow.

questions.q: There are 10^5 questions “is x prime?”, each with x ≤ 10^6. What is the best approach?
o: Sieve once, then look up each answer
Try every number up to x for each question
questions.e: The √x checks cost about 10^5 × 10^3 = 10^8 steps. One sieve up to 10^6 is about 3 × 10^6 steps, then each answer is an O(1) lookup.
